title: I tried AI for sprites and sound effects in my indie game. SFX made it in, animation didn't.
author: Jimbaceo
selftext:
Solo dev here, building a 2D game in Godot 4 with no artist or sound designer at the start. I spent a few months using AI on real assets, and the results split cleanly in two.



\*\*Sprites (ludo.ai): didn't work for me\*\*

\- Single frames often looked fine. The animation as a whole didn't.

\- Every regeneration fixed one thing and broke another. My first idle loop was almost there except for a weird mouth. On the next try the mouth changed randomly between frames. On the one after that, the mouth turned into eyes and the nose looked like an ear.

\- After burning a lot of credits, I fixed it by hand.



\*\*What I do now:\*\* AI for concept art (Gemini), then a freelance artist turns it into a proper animation. That combo works really well.



\*\*SFX (ElevenLabs): usable, with work\*\*

\- About 3 iterations per sound on average to get what I wanted.

\- Loudness was usually off for the mix, so I normalize by ear.

\- Biggest tip: keep your prompts and durations in a JSON file, with a small script that regenerates just the sounds you don't like. Re-prompting becomes cheap.



My takeaway: judge AI tools on sequences, not single outputs. One good frame or one good sound proves very little.



I wrote it up in more detail, with the failed animation loops as videos: [https://xxjoakinxx.github.io/MyBlogPost/blog/ai-for-game-assets/](https://xxjoakinxx.github.io/MyBlogPost/blog/ai-for-game-assets/)



Curious what others have seen. Has anyone gotten consistent multi-frame animation out of an AI tool, or is everyone landing on the "AI for concepts, human for animation" split?
